hubs.name: Low back pain
hubs.blurb: Including spinal stenosis in older adults

changes.text: Exercise to prevent falls now leads with dose: 3+ hours a week of challenging balance work for 12+ weeks.
Back pain prognosis adds the 2024 CMAJ update, which is less optimistic than the 2012 review.
Every card now holds its studies, each with its design, size and rating. Tap "studies" on any card.

cards.title: Exercise to prevent falls
cards.takeaway: Dose decides the result: 3+ hours a week of challenging balance work, kept up for 12+ weeks.
cards.note: Larger effects when a health professional, usually a PT, delivers it. For your plan of care: progress balance until it is truly challenging, and build a home program that gets the weekly total past 3 hours.
cards.tags: fall prevention exercise dose otago tai chi balance training hours per week detraining

studies.finding: Any exercise: falls −23% (59 trials, 12,981 people). People who fall: −15%.
3+ h/week including balance: falls −42%. Balance + functional: −24% (high). Mixed programs: −28%. Tai chi: −23% (moderate).
Challenging balance plus more than 3 h/week: falls −39%. Overall −21%.
Otago home program: falls −32%, deaths over 12 months −55%.
Balance-challenging and functional exercise, 3+ sessions a week, individualized, progressed for at least 12 weeks.
Gains are lost over 3–6 months once exercise stops, so most older adults need an ongoing program.

cards.title: Exercise that doesn't prevent falls
cards.takeaway: Walking-only, resistance-only and dance programs have not been shown to prevent falls.
cards.note: Strength work helps when it is added to balance training, not instead of it. Walking is still good for health; just don't count it as the falls program.
cards.tags: walking program resistance only dance flexibility ineffective residential care nursing home

studies.finding: Not enough evidence for programs mainly of resistance, dance or walking; none for flexibility or endurance alone.
No falls-prevention effect found in residential care, stroke survivors, or people recently discharged from hospital.
Avoid brisk walking or walking-only programs for people at risk of falls.

cards.title: Timed Up and Go (TUG)
cards.takeaway: 12 seconds or more flags fall risk. Watch how they move, not just the time.
cards.note: Shuffling, en bloc turning or steadying on walls may signal a neurological problem worth further evaluation.
cards.differ: Published cutoffs range from 12 to 16 seconds.
cards.tags: tug mobility gait steadi screen

studies.finding: Older adult taking 12 s or more is at risk of falling.

studies.cite: STEADI risk score study, BMJ Open 2023
studies.finding: Notes TUG cutoffs in the literature from 12 s to 16 s.

cards.title: 30-second chair stand
cards.takeaway: Fewer stands than the number for their age and sex means fall risk.
cards.note: Arms crossed, 17-inch seat. If they must use their arms, the score is 0.
cards.tags: 30s cst sit to stand chair rise strength norms steadi

studies.finding: Below-average score by age and sex indicates fall risk.
Original 30-s chair stand test in community-dwelling older adults.

cards.title: 4-Stage Balance Test
cards.takeaway: Can't hold tandem stance for 10 seconds = increased fall risk.
cards.note: Feet together, semi-tandem, tandem, single leg: 10 s each, no assistive device, eyes open.
cards.tags: 4 stage four stage tandem stance static balance steadi

studies.finding: Unable to hold tandem stand for at least 10 s: increased risk of falling.

cards.title: Berg Balance Scale
cards.takeaway: Don't use 45 alone: pair the score with fall history.
cards.note: The classic 45 cutoff misses about a third of fallers. MDC depends on the starting score; see Donoghue for other ranges.
cards.tags: bbs berg static dynamic balance

studies.finding: Fall history and Berg < 51, or no history and Berg < 42: 91% sensitive, 82% specific.
MDC 4.6 points when baseline is 0–24.
Cutoff 45: sensitivity 64%.
Score below 45: greater risk of falling.

cards.title: Gait speed
cards.takeaway: Under 1.0 m/s flags fall risk; 0.10 m/s is a substantial change.
cards.note: Often called the sixth vital sign.
cards.differ: After hip fracture, small meaningful change runs higher: 0.10–0.17 m/s.
cards.tags: gait speed walking speed 10mwt 4m walk sixth vital sign

studies.finding: Small meaningful change about 0.05 m/s; substantial about 0.10 m/s.
Small meaningful improvement 0.10–0.17 m/s.
1.0 m/s is the commonly applied fall-risk threshold.
0.8 m/s predicts poor clinical outcomes; 0.6 m/s further decline.

cards.title: 6MWT & SPPB change
cards.takeaway: Small change: 20 m or 0.5 pt. Substantial: 50 m or 1.0 pt.
cards.tags: 6mwt six minute walk sppb short physical performance battery endurance

studies.finding: Best initial estimates of meaningful change in older adults.

cards.title: Orthostatic hypotension
cards.takeaway: Check it: it raises fall risk about 73%. Flag a positive test to the physician.
cards.note: Lying 5 min, then measure at 1 and 3 min standing.
cards.tags: orthostatic postural hypotension blood pressure dizziness

studies.finding: Orthostatic hypotension increases fall risk 73%; protocol and cutoffs.
Systolic drop ≥ 20, diastolic drop ≥ 10, or lightheadedness from lying to standing.

cards.title: Medications & vision
cards.takeaway: Flag sedating, psychoactive, opioid and blood-pressure-lowering drugs for review.
cards.tags: medications polypharmacy frid deprescribing vision eye

studies.finding: Medication classes and vision criteria to screen.
Deprescribing high-risk drugs can reduce fall-related injuries by 35%.
In long-term care, always include rational deprescribing of fall-risk-increasing drugs.

cards.title: Who is likely to fall
cards.takeaway: Just ask: a past fall and fear of falling both predict the next one.
cards.tags: risk factors prognosis fear of falling history incidence

studies.cite: STEADI risk score study, BMJ Open 2023
studies.finding: Past-year fall OR 2.16, multiple falls OR 2.94, fear of falling OR 1.77 for falls over 4 years.
About a third of older adults at home and about half in nursing homes fall at least once a year.

cards.title: First-line care for knee OA
cards.takeaway: Exercise, weight loss and self-management first. No single exercise type beats another.
cards.note: Exercise benefit lasts up to a year; tai chi at least 24 weeks.
cards.tags: exercise strengthening aerobic weight loss tai chi self management cane brace acr arthritis foundation

studies.finding: Strong for exercise, weight loss, self-management, tai chi, cane; conditional for balance exercise.
Even 5% weight loss notably improves knee pain. No exercise type superior.

cards.title: Rehab after total knee replacement
cards.takeaway: Load the quads early and hard: high-intensity strengthening from about a week post-op, plus NMES.
cards.note: Quadriceps weakness often persists after TKA even when pain improves, which is why strengthening matters. A 2025 revision of this guideline is in progress.
cards.tags: tka total knee arthroplasty replacement nmes strength post-op cpm continuous passive motion

studies.finding: NMES, early high-intensity strength training, motor/balance training; against CPM.
Quadriceps weakness and functional limits persist after TKA.
Revision in progress; check for changes before relying on the 2020 grades.

cards.title: What doesn't help knee OA
cards.takeaway: Skip TENS. Arthroscopy is no better than exercise for degenerative knees.
cards.tags: tens arthroscopy surgery meniscus manual therapy glucosamine chondroitin prp stem cell injection

studies.finding: Strongly against TENS, chondroitin, PRP and stem cell injections; conditionally against manual therapy with exercise.
Strong recommendation against arthroscopy for nearly all degenerative knee disease.

cards.title: ACR clinical criteria, knee OA
cards.takeaway: Knee pain plus 3 of 6 findings. Works best in clear, later-stage cases.
cards.note: Age > 50, morning stiffness < 30 min, crepitus, bony tenderness, bony enlargement, no palpable warmth.
cards.differ: In a general population sample: only 41% sensitive and 75% specific.
cards.tags: acr altman criteria classification diagnosis crepitus

studies.finding: Clinical criteria: 95% sensitive, 69% specific.
41% sensitive, 75% specific; criteria mostly reflect later disease.

cards.title: OARSI performance tests
cards.takeaway: Core set: 30-second chair stand, 40 m fast walk, stair climb.
cards.note: For 30-second chair stand norms by age, see the Falls hub.
cards.tags: oarsi core set performance tests 40m fast paced walk stair climb

studies.finding: Core set and recommended set of performance tests for hip and knee OA.

cards.title: Meaningful change: chair stand & 6MWT
cards.takeaway: 2–3 more chair stands is an important gain. A 6MWT change under 61 m may be noise.
cards.differ: The chair stand value comes from hip OA, not knee OA.
cards.tags: 30s cst chair stand mcid mcii 6mwt six minute walk mdc change

studies.finding: Major clinically important improvement: 2.0–2.6 repetitions.
6MWT minimal detectable change (90%) 61.34 m.

cards.title: When it doesn't look like OA
cards.takeaway: A warm joint or morning stiffness over 30 minutes points away from OA. Consider referral.
cards.tags: inflammatory warmth stiffness referral

studies.finding: OA criteria include no palpable warmth and stiffness under 30 minutes.

cards.title: Exercise for low back pain
cards.takeaway: Older adults with chronic LBP: general exercise training is a grade A "should."
cards.tags: exercise older adults chronic acute low back pain cpg trunk activation

studies.finding: Should use general exercise for older adults with chronic LBP (A); can use exercise incl. trunk activation for acute LBP (C).

cards.title: Lumbar spinal stenosis
cards.takeaway: Best single clues: no pain when seated, and relief bending forward.
cards.note: Cluster: bilateral symptoms, leg pain more than back pain, pain walking/standing, relief sitting, age > 48. Wide-based gait has LR+ 13 but a very wide confidence interval (1.9–95).
cards.tags: lss spinal stenosis neurogenic claudication likelihood ratio romberg cluster cook

studies.finding: No pain seated LR 7.4; improvement bending forward LR 6.4; Romberg 4.2; age > 70 LR 2.0.
4 of 5 findings: LR+ 4.6, post-test probability 76%. None: LR− 0.19.

cards.title: Meaningful change in LBP
cards.takeaway: 2 points on pain, 10 on Oswestry, 5 on Roland-Morris, or 30% from baseline.
cards.note: International consensus values; treat as a starting point, not a fixed rule.
cards.tags: nprs oswestry odi roland morris rmdq mcid mic

studies.finding: NRS 2, ODI 10, Roland-Morris 5; 30% change meaningful for individual patients.

cards.title: Red flag: cancer
cards.takeaway: A history of cancer is the one red flag that really moves the needle.
cards.note: Most other red flags barely change the probability on their own. Don't rely on any one question.
cards.tags: red flag malignancy cancer metastasis screening

studies.finding: History of malignancy: highest post-test probability (33%).
Don't base suspicion of malignancy on one red flag question.

cards.title: Red flag: spinal fracture
cards.takeaway: Older age, long-term steroids, major trauma, or a bruise or abrasion. Several together are serious.
cards.tags: fracture compression osteoporosis steroids trauma red flag

studies.finding: Multiple red flags: 90% probability of fracture (wide CI 34–99%).

cards.title: Expected course of LBP
cards.takeaway: Acute pain roughly halves in 6 weeks, but many still have some pain at a year.
cards.note: Useful for setting expectations: early gains are fast, then progress slows.
cards.differ: The 2012 review was more optimistic (acute pain 6/100 at a year). The 2024 update is larger and newer.
cards.tags: prognosis natural history recovery timeline course

studies.finding: Acute pain 56 → 26 at 6 weeks → 21 at 1 year. Persistent 56 → 48 → 40.
Acute pain 52 → 23 at 6 weeks → 6 at 1 year. Persistent 51 → 33 → 23.
